lesson.title: The second cut runs across every piece

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the pieces stay unequal, 3 kept of 7, until the second cut crosses the unshaded quarter and the whole becomes 8 equal pieces, 3/8, when you run the cut across all four quarters.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A rectangle, the whole, standing for a circuit's full rated load, say 32 A. It is cut into four equal upright strips, the quarters, and the left three are shaded: the three-quarter load. At the opening setting nothing else has happened: the label beneath the rectangle reads 3/4, nothing taken yet, and the readouts give 4 pieces, 0 kept and 0 A. The slider runs a second cut across the rectangle from the left, through the quarters already there: at 1 it has crossed the first quarter, at 3 the three shaded ones, at 4 the unshaded quarter as well, from side to side. With A half chosen the second cut is one line, splitting each quarter it crosses into two equal rows; for A third or Two thirds it is two lines making three rows, and for A quarter or Three quarters three lines making four. In each shaded quarter the cut has crossed, the top rows are hatched, as many as the chosen fraction's top says: one row of two for a half, two of three for two-thirds. That hatched part is the kept part, the fraction of the three-quarters you are taking, and the label says what the picture can honestly call it. The readouts count the pieces in the whole, the pieces kept, and the load the kept part stands for.

The rule, from the pieces. Pieces in the whole = the quarters not yet crossed, 4 minus the slider, plus each crossed quarter times the rows the cut makes: with a half it reads 4, then 5, 6, 7, then 4 × 2 = 8 at 4. Only at 0 and at 4 are the pieces all the same size, so only there does the picture have a bottom number; in between, the label gives the count and says the pieces are unequal, 3 of 7 pieces, not equal. Pieces kept = the shaded quarters crossed, the slider up to 3, times the rows kept, the chosen fraction's top: 3 × 1 = 3 for a half. At 4 the label reads them as a fraction, pieces kept over pieces in the whole, 3/8, which is 3 × 1 over 4 × 2, the tops multiplied over the bottoms multiplied; where a number goes into both it adds the simpler name, 6/12 = 1/2 for two-thirds. The load readout is worked from amounts, not from the count: a quarter of 32 A is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 A, each crossed shaded quarter keeps the chosen fraction of that, 8 ÷ 2 = 4 A for a half, so the load kept is 4 A times the shaded quarters crossed, 12 A once the cut is past the third quarter, and still 12 A at 4, where 3/8 of 32 A is 3 × (32 ÷ 8) = 12 A. The end readings for the other choices: a third, 3/12 and 8 A; two-thirds, 6/12 and 16 A; a quarter, 3/16 and 6 A; three-quarters, 9/16 and 18 A.
interactive.ignores: The cut runs from the left and the shaded quarters are the left three, so the kept load is complete one step before its name is; that order is a drawing choice, and the name needs all four quarters crossed whichever end the cut starts from. The kept rows are drawn at the top; any rows would do, since equal rows are the same amount. The whole is drawn as an area and a load is not a shape, but a fraction's whole can be anything that can be shared equally. Cuts are drawn with no width, so the pieces are exact. One first fraction, three-quarters, is shown, and the fractions taken are all under one; the same cutting works for any first fraction, and taking more than one of something, three halves of it, would need a second whole drawn beside the first. The 32 A is a chosen rating, and a real circuit's load moves about from minute to minute.

explain.text:
Half of three-quarters of a circuit's load is three-eighths of it: 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. The reason is in where the second cut falls. Remember from 'Four pieces are not four quarters' that the bottom number is honest only when every piece is equal, and from 'One mark, many names' that cutting every piece into the same number of smaller pieces renames a fraction without moving it? Taking a fraction of a fraction is those two moves, one after the other.

'Of' means multiply here:[^1] half of three-quarters is three-quarters times a half, and that is three-eighths.[^2] Area is a standard way to picture multiplying two fractions,[^3] so picture the circuit's full rated load as a rectangle cut into four equal quarters, three of them shaded: the three-quarter load. Now take half of the shaded part. A half is one of two equal pieces, so a second cut splits the shaded quarters into two equal rows and you keep one row. That already fixes the amount. But to call the kept part a fraction of the whole, the whole must be in equal pieces, because a fraction's whole is divided into equal parts,[^4] and a cut that stopped at the shaded quarters would leave six half-quarters and one quarter still whole, seven pieces of two sizes with no bottom number. So the second cut runs on through the unshaded quarter too. Now every quarter is cut in two, the whole has 4 × 2 = 8 equal pieces, eighths, and the three shaded quarters have become 3 × 2 = 6 of them: 3/4 renamed as 6/8 without moving, top and bottom multiplied by the same 2.[^5] The kept row of those six eighths is 3 × 1 = 3 pieces: three of the whole's eight equal pieces, 3/8. **To take a fraction of a fraction, multiply the tops for the new top and the bottoms for the new bottom, then simplify where a number goes into both.**[^6][^7] The bottoms multiplied, 4 × 2, because the second cut crosses every piece the first cut made, so each of the 4 quarters becomes 2 pieces; the tops multiplied, 3 × 1, because the kept part is 3 shaded quarters wide and 1 of the 2 rows tall, which is 3 × 1 small pieces.

Check it in amps. Say the circuit is rated at 32 A. A quarter of that is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 A, so the three-quarter load is 3 × 8 = 24 A and half of it is 12 A. Now 3/8 of 32 A: an eighth is 32 ÷ 8 = 4 A and three of them are 12 A. The two routes agree. The same cutting works for any pair. Two-thirds of three-quarters: the second cut splits every quarter into three rows, 4 × 3 = 12 twelfths, and you keep two rows of the three shaded quarters, 3 × 2 = 6 pieces, 6/12, which is 1/2 once top and bottom are divided by 6, the renaming run backwards. In amps, two-thirds of 24 A is 16 A, and half of 32 A is 16 A. Whenever the fraction you take is less than a whole, the answer is smaller than the fraction you took it from, because you keep some of the rows and not all of them. Half of two-fifths is two-tenths, which is a fifth.[^8]

The habit that fails here comes from the last lesson. Adding needed one piece size first, so it is tempting to match the pieces before multiplying too: 1/2 is 2/4, and 2/4 × 3/4 = 6/4. That is a whole and a half of the rating, 48 A on a 32 A circuit, from taking half of a three-quarter load, and half of something cannot be more than the thing. The renaming itself does no harm, 2/4 × 3/4 = 6/16 is 3/8 again; the damage is keeping the bottom, as adding does. Adding keeps the bottom because it counts pieces of one size, and the piece does not change when you count more of it. Multiplying by a fraction does not count pieces, it cuts them, and the bottom has to grow with the cut. The other habit is the one the slider shows at three quarters crossed: reading the picture before the cut has crossed every piece, 3 pieces kept out of 7, and calling it 3/7. The kept part is the right amount, 12 A, but 3/7 of 32 A is about 13.7 A, because the picture holds pieces of two sizes and a count of unequal pieces is not a bottom number; cross the last quarter and the honest name, 3/8, appears.

**A fraction of a fraction multiplies, tops by tops and bottoms by bottoms, because the second cut runs across every piece the first cut made: half of three-quarters is 3/8, and the 8 is there because all four quarters were cut in two.[^2][^6]**

analogy.text: You already multiply rating factors. Say a cable's tabled current rating has to be cut to 0.8 of itself for grouping and then to 0.9 of that for the air temperature around it. You multiply, 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, and you do not add them or take the worse of the two, because the second factor takes its share of what the first factor left. Write them as fractions and it is this lesson's picture: 8/10 of the rating, then 9/10 of that, 8 × 9 = 72 pieces kept out of 10 × 10 = 100, so 72/100 of the tabled rating, tops by tops and bottoms by bottoms, and smaller than either factor on its own.
analogy.breaks: The factors come from tables and nothing is being cut: the cable is not in pieces, so there is no shape to check the count against, and a decimal hides its bottom number the way a unit does, so you have to supply the tenths yourself to see the 10 × 10. And both factors here are under one, like every fraction the picture takes; a fraction bigger than one, three halves of a load, gives more than you started with and would need a second whole drawn beside the first.

practice.text:
Taking a fraction of a fraction (a share of a load, part of what is left on a drum, a part of a part of an hour):
- Read 'of' as multiply: half of three-quarters is 1/2 × 3/4.
- Put every number in fraction form first: a whole number goes over 1 (3 is 3/1); a mixed number becomes an improper fraction (1 1/2 is 3/2).
- Multiply the tops for the new top and the bottoms for the new bottom. Do not match the pieces first: that is the adding move.
- Simplify where one number goes into both: 6/12 is 1/2. If the top is bigger than the bottom, read it as a mixed number: 9/2 is 4 1/2.
- Check the size: a fraction under one of something gives less than you started with, and a fraction over one gives more. Where you can, check in units: amps, metres, minutes.

**Rule of thumb:** tops by tops, bottoms by bottoms, nothing to match. Before you simplify, the new bottom is the two old bottoms multiplied; a bottom that simply stayed, when neither old bottom was 1, means you kept one, as adding does.

**Worked example:** a 50 m drum has two-fifths of its cable left, and the next run needs three-quarters of what is left. 3/4 × 2/5: tops 3 × 2 = 6, bottoms 4 × 5 = 20, so 6/20 of the drum, which is 3/10 once both are divided by 2. In metres: a fifth of 50 m is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 m, so 20 m is left; three-quarters of 20 m is 15 m; and 3/10 of 50 m is 15 m. Agreed. With a whole number: three visits of 1 1/2 hours is 3/1 × 3/2 = 9/2 hours, 4 1/2 hours; the bottom stayed 2 because the 3 brought a 1 underneath.

**Common mistakes:**
- Matching the pieces first and then keeping the bottom, 2/4 × 3/4 = 6/4: bigger than the three-quarters you took a part of. Matching is for adding.
- Multiplying across, the top of one by the bottom of the other: 1/2 × 3/4 as 4/6. Tops go with tops.
- Giving a whole number a bottom it does not have: 2 × 3/4 as 6/8, which is 3/4 again, so the doubling vanished. 2 is 2/1, so 2 × 3/4 = 6/4 = 1 1/2.
- Expecting multiplying to make more. With whole numbers above one it did, because two lots of something is more than one lot; half a lot is less, so half of 24 A is 12 A.
- Reading a count off unequal pieces: 3 of 7 pieces is 3/7 only if the seven are equal. The second cut runs across every piece.
- Mixing wholes: 3/8 is of the circuit's full rating, 32 A, not of the 24 A load. Say which whole each fraction is of.

checks.label: Nothing crossed: 4 quarters, 0 pieces kept, 0 A, and the label reads 3/4
For a half the pieces in the whole climb 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 as the cut crosses each quarter, 3 + 1 × 2 = 5 and so on, and only at 0 and 4 crossed are they all equal
At 4 crossed for a half, 3 × 1 = 3 pieces kept of 4 × 2 = 8: the label reads 3/8
Half of three-quarters is three-quarters multiplied by a half, three-eighths
By amounts, 3 crossed shaded quarters keep 3 × (8 ÷ 2) = 12 A, still 12 A at 4 crossed; 3/8 of 32 A is 3 × 4 = 12 A too, while 3/7 of 32 A would be about 13.7 A
The ends for the other choices: a third 3/12 = 1/4 and 8 A, two thirds 6/12 = 1/2 and 16 A, a quarter 3/16 and 6 A, three quarters 9/16 and 18 A
Keeping the bottom, 2/4 × 3/4 = 6/4, would mean 48 A on a 32 A circuit; the kept part never exceeds the 24 A shaded load
The label names a fraction of the whole only while every piece of the whole is equal

applied.problem: "Multiplying does not count pieces, it cuts them, and the bottom has to grow with the cut" fails for a whole-number multiplier (3/1 × 3/2 keeps bottom 2, as the practice itself shows); read alone on a card it is false, so narrow it to multiplying by a fraction.

The rule of thumb says a bottom that stayed means you kept one as adding does, yet the worked example rightly keeps bottom 2 when a whole number (bottom 1) multiplies; and "with whole numbers it did" make more is false for 1 and 0, so both claims need narrowing.
